title: The Traditional Way of Saving Money Versus the Modern Style of Investment: The Financial Management Styles of Sorsogon State University (Sorsu) Bulan Campus Faculty Members
authors: Bongalonta, M. B.; Bongalonta, M. M.; Gigantoca, S. E.
venue: International Journal of Multidisciplinary: Applied Business and Education Research
tldr: A mixed-methods study of 40 Filipino faculty members found that both traditional saving methods and modern investments are adopted, while rising costs, poor debt management, and low financial literacy hinder saving capacity.
problem_and_motivation: Faculty members at Philippine state universities face significant financial challenges including low salaries, rising living costs, and poor financial literacy, yet their saving practices and the barriers they encounter remain underexplored.
approach: Mixed-methods design combining a survey of 40 SorSU Bulan Campus faculty members with focus group discussions to capture both quantitative profiles and qualitative insights.
Quantitative component collected demographic and financial data including age, gender, salary grade, income, expenses, appointment status, savings percentage, and saving modalities.
Qualitative FGDs used semi-structured interview guides to explore saving practices, problems encountered, and factors influencing financial decisions.
FGD data were transcribed and coded using open coding to identify emergent themes and patterns in saving behavior and financial challenges.
A four-step financial management model was formulated from the results, covering budgeting, debt minimization, emergency saving, and retirement investment.
findings: num: 60% of respondents set aside only 0-15% of their total income as savings.
num: 62.5% of respondents earn PHP 40,001-50,000 monthly, above the national median.
num: 82.5% of respondents incur monthly expenses exceeding PHP 12,000.
num: 30% of faculty save via piggy banks and 30% via time deposits.
Faculty adopt both traditional methods (piggy bank, paluwagan, budgeting) and modern investments (stocks, time deposits, properties).
Rising utility costs and unexpected expenses were the most commonly cited barriers to saving.
Poor debt management through GSIS and Land Bank loans significantly depleted faculty savings capacity.
Lack of financial literacy was reported as a fundamental barrier preventing faculty from making informed financial decisions.
Delayed and insufficient salaries particularly affected non-permanent faculty members ability to save.
num: Default rates in paluwagan systems can range from 5% to 50% depending on group size and contribution frequency.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes empirical data on the saving practices and financial challenges of Filipino faculty members at a Philippine state university.
directly_justifies: Faculty members adopt both traditional saving methods and modern investment styles for their finances.
Rising utility costs and unexpected day-to-day expenses are primary barriers to saving for faculty.
Poor debt management through institutional loans significantly reduces faculty savings capacity.
Lack of financial literacy prevents faculty from making informed saving and investment decisions.
num: 60% of respondents set aside only 0-15% of their income as savings.
limits: Small sample size of 40 faculty members from a single campus limits generalizability to broader populations.
No validated financial literacy instrument was administered, relying only on self-reported perceptions.
The proposed financial management model lacks empirical validation or controlled testing.
The study does not control for confounding variables such as household size or dependents.
